findings.title: Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
findings.body: The ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, making all cleanup jobs, including the batched annotation cleanup, run ten times as often. This is unrelated to splitting the annotation queries and can increase sustained database load, lock contention, and the chance of overlapping long-running cleanup work (the per-run timeout is 9 minutes). The interval should remain 10 minutes unless this change is intentional and justified.

findings.title: Routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists
findings.body: Every batch in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs via r.log.Error, including successful batches and empty batches, and includes the complete ids slice and SQL condition. This will emit error-level records on every cleanup cycle, polluting error monitoring, and with large batch sizes (for example the 32767 case added in tests) creates very large log lines. Routine progress should be Debug/Info and should log counts, not all IDs.

findings.title: Parameter-limit handling only special-cases SQLite and can stall cleanup on other databases
findings.body: deleteByIDs builds one bind parameter per ID for every non-SQLite database. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured above the driver's parameter limit (for example SQL Server's 2100 or MySQL/PostgreSQL prepared-statement limits), the DELETE fails and untilDoneOrCancelled aborts, so cleanup cannot progress in subsequent batches. The previous subquery DELETE had no per-ID parameter limit. The delete should be chunked below the dialect's limit, or inlined/chunked safely for all supported databases, not only when SQLite's batch size exceeds 999.

findings.title: SQLite ID list construction is quadratic for large batches
findings.body: The SQLite branch builds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop, repeatedly copying the growing string. For the tested batch size of 32767 this is O(n^2) copying and can allocate substantial memory/CPU on every batch. Use strings.Builder (already imported) or strconv.AppendInt into a byte buffer to build the list in linear time.
